  The determination of parton distribution functions (PDFs) from experimental data relies on the theoretical framework of perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). This framework is implemented through the DGLAP evolution equations, which are solved numerically to generate the PDFs. This study introduces a Python-based framework that automates the entire procedure, from solving the DGLAP equations to computing cross-sections and performing the fit. It is also capable of handling both fixed-order and next-to-leading-logarithmic (NLL) calculations. We examine the recurrence times of X-ray transients in neutron star (NS) binaries, focusing on the correlation between the time elapsed since the last outburst and the duration of the subsequent one. Our analysis of 11 NS binaries with known recurrence times reveals a strong positive correlation, suggesting that the time since the previous outburst influences the duration of the next. This finding supports the hypothesis that the accretion disk's lifetime is governed by the time required to clear the disk of material accumulated during the preceding outburst. Furthermore, we investigate the nature of the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre, which are believed to be NS binaries. We find that the recurrence times for these systems are significantly longer than those for NS binaries in the Milky Way disk, implying that the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are likely low-mass X-ray binaries rather than NS binaries. Additionally, we explore the possibility that the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are actually NS binaries with unusually long recurrence times. If this were true, the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre would represent the most extreme examples of NS binaries in the Milky Way. However, we argue that this scenario is unlikely, as it would require the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre to have recurrence times exceeding 100,000 years, which is inconsistent with the observed distribution of recurrence times for NS binaries in the Milky Way disk. Consequently, we conclude that the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are low-mass X-ray binaries. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the formation of NS binaries in the Galactic Centre.

This paper introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique for reducing CPU frequency to achieve significant energy savings. Unlike existing methods that rely on hardware support for frequency scaling, HyperDegrade operates entirely in software, making it applicable to any CPU. The approach leverages the CPU's ability to execute instructions at lower frequencies by utilizing the instruction cache to store frequently used instructions. This allows the CPU to run at reduced frequencies while maintaining performance comparable to higher frequencies. We evaluated HyperDegrade on a 1.2 GHz CPU, demonstrating that it can achieve effective frequencies ranging from 1.2 GHz down to 100 MHz. Our results indicate that HyperDegrade can reduce energy consumption by up to 90% compared to the original frequency, with a performance penalty of only 10% at 100 MHz. Furthermore, we developed a dynamic version of HyperDegrade that automatically adjusts the effective frequency based on the application's performance requirements. This dynamic approach can lower energy usage by up to 70% while incurring a performance penalty of just 1%.

Optical character recognition (OCR) is frequently employed to tally votes from paper ballots, yet its accuracy remains a significant concern. This study introduces iOCR, a novel OCR system specifically designed for election ballots. Unlike conventional OCR methods, iOCR leverages the inherent structure of ballots to enhance recognition precision. It employs a two-stage process: first, it identifies the text regions on the ballot, and second, it utilizes a deep learning model to recognize the text within those regions. The system was evaluated on 1,000 ballots from the 2016 and 2018 U.S. elections, achieving an average character-level accuracy of 99.9% and a word-level accuracy of 99.8%. Furthermore, iOCR was tested on 1,000 ballots from the 2020 U.S. election, demonstrating a 99.9% character-level accuracy and a 99.8% word-level accuracy. These results indicate that iOCR can reliably extract text from ballots, thereby supporting the development of more accurate vote-counting systems. The source code for iOCR is available at https://github.com/ai4e/iOCR.

Paired-permutation tests are a standard method for assessing the significance of test statistics derived from paired data, such as those found in clinical trials or before-and-after studies. While the exact distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis is theoretically known, it is often computationally infeasible to calculate for complex statistics. Consequently, researchers typically rely on Monte Carlo simulations to approximate the distribution. This study introduces a novel approach to compute the exact distribution of the test statistic for a broad class of structured statistics, including the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the sign test, and the paired t-test. The method is demonstrated to be efficient for these statistics and is also applicable to other structured statistics. Furthermore, the approach is extended to handle the case where the null hypothesis is composite. The findings are illustrated using data from a clinical trial evaluating the efficacy of a new drug for treating depression.

We establish that the solitary wave is spectrally stable for all coupling constants $\alpha$ within the range $0 < \alpha < \alpha_{\text{max}}$, where $\alpha_{\text{max}}$ is the value at which the solitary wave ceases to exist. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solitary wave is orbitally stable for all $\alpha$ in the interval $0 < \alpha < \alpha_{\text{max}}$. These findings are derived through a combination of abstract spectral analysis and the application of the Vakhitov--Kolokolov stability criterion. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the solitary wave's behavior as $\alpha$ approaches $\alpha_{\text{max}}$. Finally, we present numerical results indicating that the solitary wave is spectrally unstable for $\alpha > \alpha_{\text{max}}$.

We investigate the potential for the Belle II experiment to detect axion-like particles (ALPs) produced in $B$ meson decays. We examine the kinematic constraints on ALP production and decay, and determine the optimal decay channels for ALPs with masses ranging from 100 MeV to 10 GeV. We also assess the sensitivity of the Belle II detector to these ALPs, considering both displaced and invisible decay modes. Our findings indicate that the displaced decay channel offers the most promising avenue for detection, with the most favorable decay modes being $a \to \gamma\gamma$ and $a \to \pi^0\pi^0$. For the invisible decay channel, the most sensitive modes are $a \to \nu\bar{\nu}$ and $a \to \gamma\gamma$. We further analyze the sensitivity of the displaced decay channel to ALPs with masses between 100 MeV and 1 GeV, assuming the decay $a \to \gamma\gamma$ is the dominant mode. This analysis relies on the $B^0 \to K^{*0}a$ decay, where the $K^{*0}$ subsequently decays into $K^+\pi^-$. We find that the displaced decay channel is the most sensitive for ALP masses below 1 GeV, whereas the invisible decay channel becomes more sensitive for masses exceeding 1 GeV. Finally, we compare the sensitivity of the displaced decay channel to the invisible decay channel for ALP masses between 100 MeV and 1 GeV, assuming the decay $a \to \pi^0\pi^0$ is the dominant mode. This comparison utilizes the $B^0 \to K^{*0}a$ decay, with the $K^{*0}$ decaying into $K^+\pi^-$. We conclude that the displaced decay channel is more sensitive than the invisible decay channel for ALP masses below 1 GeV, while the invisible decay channel is more sensitive for masses above 1 GeV.

Semantic change detection (SCD) involves identifying shifts in word meanings over time, a task that is crucial for understanding how language evolves. While recent studies have shown that contextualized language models (LMs) can effectively detect these changes, the specific mechanisms behind their success remain unclear. This paper investigates the performance of contextualized LMs on SCD tasks and examines the factors influencing their effectiveness. We find that the performance of these models is highly dependent on the specific task and the type of semantic change involved. Furthermore, we observe that the models' ability to detect changes is closely tied to the quality of the training data. Finally, we demonstrate that the models' performance is significantly affected by the choice of hyperparameters. These findings offer valuable insights for future research on SCD and the application of contextualized LMs to other tasks.

We examine the spin evolution of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) within the context of ultralight boson models, utilizing the observed spins of heavy quasars. Our findings indicate that the spin evolution of SMBHs is significantly influenced by the presence of ultralight bosons. Specifically, we observe that the spin of SMBHs is suppressed by the boson field, and the spin evolution of SMBHs is notably affected by the boson field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spin evolution of SMBHs is sensitive to the mass of the boson field. Consequently, the spin evolution of SMBHs can serve as a probe for the mass of the boson field. Additionally, we show that the spin evolution of SMBHs is sensitive to the initial spin of the SMBH. Finally, we find that the spin evolution of SMBHs is sensitive to the accretion rate. These results suggest that the spin evolution of SMBHs can be used to constrain the mass of the boson field.

The vector magnetic field is a fundamental parameter for understanding solar physics, yet its measurement remains challenging. While the Spectral Line Inversion Code (SPIN) has been developed to infer this field from spectropolarimetric observations, the resulting measurements are susceptible to systematic biases. This study investigates the origins of these biases and evaluates the efficacy of the SPIN bias mitigation strategy. We demonstrate that the primary source of bias stems from the assumption of a uniform magnetic field within the pixel, which fails to account for the actual magnetic field distribution. Furthermore, we show that the SPIN bias mitigation approach is effective in reducing these biases. Finally, we introduce a novel method to quantify the bias in inferred measurements, which can be applied to any inversion code. This method relies on the assumption that the magnetic field distribution within the pixel follows a Gaussian profile. We validate this approach using synthetic data and apply it to real observations from the Dunn Solar Telescope. The results indicate that the bias in inferred measurements is substantial, particularly in regions with strong magnetic fields. Consequently, the bias mitigation strategy is essential for obtaining accurate measurements.

This study investigates the effects of using alternative loss functions, specifically the exponential loss and the hinge loss, on the performance of deep learning models. Our findings indicate that the exponential loss function can outperform cross-entropy in specific contexts, whereas the hinge loss generally yields inferior results. This study introduces a novel approach to video prediction that leverages a dual representation of the input video. The first representation is a standard video sequence, while the second is a sequence of images captured from a novel viewpoint. We hypothesize that the novel view sequence contains valuable information for predicting the future of the standard video. To test this, we developed a model that learns to predict the future of the standard video using both the standard video sequence and the novel view sequence. We evaluated our method on the KITTI dataset, which features videos from both standard and novel viewpoints. Our results indicate that incorporating the novel view sequence significantly enhances the accuracy of the standard video prediction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed method can be applied to the KITTI dataset to generate novel view videos from standard view videos.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$ is defined as the smallest cardinality of a resolving set for $G$. This paper introduces the truncated metric dimension, denoted as $\beta_{\tau}(G)$, which represents the minimum size of a set $S$ such that the distance between any two vertices in $G$ can be uniquely determined by their distances to the elements of $S$, provided these distances do not exceed $\tau$. We establish that $\beta_{\tau}(G)$ is bounded below by the metric dimension of $G$ and above by the metric dimension of the $\tau$-th power of $G$. Furthermore, we derive a lower bound for $\beta_{\tau}(G)$ in terms of the metric dimension of the $\tau$-th power of $G$. We also examine the relationship between $\beta_{\tau}(G)$ and the metric dimension of the $\tau$-th power of $G$ for specific graph classes, including trees, cycles, and complete graphs. Finally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for computing $\beta_{\tau}(G)$ when $G$ is a tree.

The primary objective of this study is to develop a deep learning model capable of classifying heart sounds into four distinct categories: normal, mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, and aortic regurgitation. The model is designed to be robust against additive noise and convolutional distortion. To achieve this, we employed a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that incorporates a noise reduction module and a distortion reduction module. The noise reduction module utilizes a denoising autoencoder, while the distortion reduction module employs a distortion autoencoder. We evaluated the model's performance using the PhysioNet/CinC 2016 Challenge dataset, which contains 1,000 heart sound recordings. The results indicate that the proposed model outperforms the baseline model in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Furthermore, the model demonstrates superior performance compared to the baseline when tested on noisy and distorted data. These findings suggest that the proposed model is effective for classifying heart sounds under conditions of additive noise and convolutional distortion.

The C{\sc i} 1--0 and 2--1 transitions are the primary tracers of molecular gas in galaxies, yet their excitation mechanisms remain uncertain. While the 1--0 transition is widely assumed to be subthermally excited, the 2--1 transition is often treated as thermally excited, a premise that may not hold for low-metallicity galaxies. We present a detailed analysis of the C{\sc i} 1--0 and 2--1 transitions in the molecular gas reservoirs of 11 galaxies, utilizing data from the ALMA Large Program for the C{\sc i} 1--0 and 2--1 transitions in the Molecular Gas Reservoirs of Galaxies (ALMA-11). Our findings indicate that the 2--1 transition is subthermally excited in all galaxies, with the 2--1/1--0 ratio ranging from 0.1 to 0.5. This ratio correlates with the C{\sc i} 1--0 luminosity, suggesting that the 2--1 transition is subthermally excited in low-metallicity galaxies. Consequently, the 2--1 transition serves as a reliable tracer of molecular gas in low-metallicity environments. Furthermore, the C{\sc i} 1--0 and 2--1 transitions are more sensitive to the molecular gas reservoirs than the CO 1--0 transition, as the C{\sc i} 1--0 luminosity correlates with the CO 1--0 luminosity, whereas the CO 1--0 luminosity does not correlate with the C{\sc i} 1--0 luminosity. This study demonstrates that the C{\sc i} 1--0 and 2--1 transitions are valuable tools for investigating the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies.

We introduce the speed process for the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) on the integers, defined as the difference between the number of particles to the left and right of a specific site. This process is shown to be a Markov chain with a transition matrix that is tridiagonal and non-negative. We establish that the speed process is ergodic and determine its stationary distribution. Furthermore, we derive the transition rates for the speed process and demonstrate that it corresponds to a specific instance of the $q$-Hahn process. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the speed process for the ASEP on the half-line.

Finally, the paper outlines the essential components of a robust model and the necessary steps to ensure its reliability. Sentiment analysis is a critical task in natural language processing, yet it remains challenging to perform across multiple languages. While existing cross-lingual methods often rely on parallel corpora, these resources are frequently unavailable for low-resource languages. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel multi-task learning framework that leverages monolingual data to enhance cross-lingual sentiment analysis. Our approach utilizes a shared encoder to extract features from both the target and source languages, while employing distinct decoders for each language. We evaluate our method on the Sentiment140 dataset, which contains English and Spanish tweets, and on the SemEval-2014 Task 4 dataset, which includes English, French, and German tweets. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 1.5% improvement on the English-Spanish task and a 2.5% improvement on the English-German task. Furthermore, our method surpasses the performance of the best-performing model on the English-French task. These findings indicate that our approach is effective for cross-lingual sentiment analysis, particularly for low-resource languages. The code is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/Multi-task-Learning-for-Cross-Lingual-Sentiment-Analysis.

The rapid rotation of the surface of the star $\kappa$ Ceti, which is approximately 1.5 times the mass of the Sun, presents a significant puzzle. This star is currently in the main sequence phase, yet its surface rotation period is only 1.5 days, implying a spin-up of roughly 100 times compared to the Sun. This acceleration is far more extreme than what is observed in the Sun or other stars of similar mass. While the star's rotation rate is consistent with the predictions of the Skumanich law for stars with convective envelopes, the mechanism driving this rapid spin-up remains unclear. We propose that the star's rotation was accelerated by the engulfment of a planet, which transferred angular momentum to the star. This scenario aligns with the star's observed rotation rate and the presence of a debris disk. Furthermore, the star's rotation period is consistent with the timescale required for the planet to spiral into the star. We also examine the possibility that the star's rotation was accelerated by magnetic braking, which would require an unusually high magnetic field strength. Finally, we discuss the implications of this finding for the angular momentum evolution of solar-type stars.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, yet they often struggle with specific tasks requiring specialized knowledge. While fine-tuning on domain-specific data is a common approach, it is frequently impractical due to the scarcity of labeled data and the high costs associated with training. To address this, we introduce SKILL, a method that integrates structured knowledge into LLMs via a novel knowledge infusion technique. SKILL employs a two-stage process: first, it extracts knowledge from a knowledge graph and converts it into a structured format; second, it infuses this structured knowledge into the LLM using a specialized prompt. We evaluate SKILL on three distinct tasks: question answering, text classification, and named entity recognition. Our results indicate that SKILL significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a 10.5% improvement in F1 score for question answering, a 10.1% increase in accuracy for text classification, and a 10.2% gain in F1 score for named entity recognition. Furthermore, SKILL surpasses the performance of the LLMs used for knowledge extraction, demonstrating that structured knowledge infusion can enhance LLMs even when the underlying models are not state-of-the-art. The code for SKILL is available at https://github.com/Cheng-Yu-Lin/SKILL.

By employing the shadow formalism, we derive the shadow temperature and shadow entropy for these black holes. Our analysis reveals that the shadow temperature is directly proportional to the Hawking temperature, while the shadow entropy is proportional to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Furthermore, we examine the shadow phase transition of these black holes and find that the shadow phase transition temperature is proportional to the Hawking temperature. Finally, we demonstrate that the shadow phase transition temperature is independent of the non-linear parameter. These findings suggest that the shadow formalism can be utilized to study the thermodynamic properties of black holes.

This study examines the evolution of entanglement and synchronization within a two-mode quantum system, specifically focusing on the transition from a separable state to a synchronized state. We analyze the system's behavior across the separable, entangled, and synchronized regimes using the tomographic representation of the density operator. The peeling of an adhesive tape is a classic example of a driven interface problem, where the interface between the tape and the substrate exhibits a rough, fractal-like morphology. This study investigates the acoustic emission generated during the peeling process, which is characterized by a broad power-law distribution of event magnitudes. We demonstrate that the acoustic emission displays a hidden order, which we term crackling noise. This noise is governed by a power-law distribution of event magnitudes and a specific scaling relation between the event magnitude and its duration. Furthermore, we observe that the acoustic emission is composed of distinct events, each corresponding to a specific segment of the interface. The magnitude of these events is directly linked to the length of the interface segment involved. Finally, we show that the acoustic emission is influenced by the peeling velocity, with the power-law exponent of the event magnitude distribution varying as a function of this velocity. This allows the model to execute a specific, attacker-defined action when the trigger is present, while maintaining normal behavior otherwise. Furthermore, we show that the dynamic backdoor remains undetectable by existing detection methods. To address this vulnerability, we propose a defense mechanism that utilizes the GAP layer to identify and mitigate the dynamic backdoor. Experimental results indicate that our defense successfully neutralizes the attack, restoring the model's performance to its original state.

However, the performance of FL is significantly impacted by data heterogeneity, which arises from the non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-IID) nature of data across devices. This study introduces a novel FL framework that leverages random walks to mitigate the effects of data heterogeneity. The proposed method, termed Walk for Learning (WFL), employs a random walk strategy to facilitate the exchange of model parameters among devices. This study addresses the inverse problem of determining the shape of a rigid body from the acoustic pressure field generated by a point source located within the body. The analysis is conducted in the frequency domain, where the pressure field is governed by the Helmholtz equation. The primary objective is to establish the uniqueness of the solution for this inverse problem. To achieve this, we employ the method of conformal mapping to transform the problem into a domain with a known geometry, thereby reducing the problem to a boundary value problem for the Helmholtz equation. The uniqueness of the solution for this transformed problem is then proven using the unique continuation property of the Helmholtz equation. Finally, we demonstrate that the solution to the original inverse problem is unique by applying the uniqueness of the solution to the transformed problem.

We examine the minimal scoto-seesaw framework, which incorporates a single scalar singlet and a single fermion doublet to generate neutrino masses. This study focuses on the phenomenology of the scalar singlet, which serves as the dark matter candidate. We analyze the dark matter relic density, direct detection constraints, and indirect detection signals. Furthermore, we investigate the vacuum stability of the scalar potential and the stability of the electroweak vacuum. Our findings indicate that the dark matter relic density can be achieved through the freeze-out mechanism, while direct detection limits are satisfied via the $Z$-boson portal. Additionally, the dark matter candidate can be detected via the decay of the scalar singlet into neutrinos. Finally, we demonstrate that the vacuum stability of the scalar potential is maintained up to the Planck scale.
